blocks.text: Pliny, writing to Clemens about the son of Regulus in Letter 2 of book 4: "The boy had many ponies, both harnessed and unharnessed; he had dogs large and small; he had nightingales, parrots, blackbirds." Julius Capitolinus in Clodius Albinus: "Seven small eagles were brought from the nest and placed, as if in play, around the boy's cradle." Pausanias in the Corinthiaca: Κόκκυγα δὲ ἐπὶ τῷ σκήπτρῳ καθῆσθαί φασι, λέγοντες [II, 729] τὸν Δία, ὅτε ἤρα παρθένου τῆς Ἥρας ἐς τοῦτον τὸν ὄρνιθα ἀλλαγῆναι· τὴν δὲ ἅτε παίγνιον θηρᾶσαι· [Kokkyga de epi tō skēptrō kathēsthai phasi, legontes ton Dia, hote ēra parthenou tēs Hēras es touton ton ornitha allagēnai; tēn de hate paignion thērasai] "They say the cuckoo sits on the sceptre of Jove because Jupiter, seized with love for the maiden Juno, turned himself into that bird, which the girl caught as a plaything." Hence Jupiter Coccygius, whom the same author mentions further on. Accordingly Jerome explains the passage of Job we mentioned thus: "Will you play with him as with a bird? Or will you bind him for your maidservants?", making no mention of a sparrow. And most of the more recent interpreters follow the same.

III. The third passage is Psal. X, 1. (in the Hebrew XI, 1.), where the Greek version has Μεταναστεύου ἐπὶ τὰ ὄρη ὡς στρουθίον· [Metanasteuou epi ta orē hōs strouthion], and the Vulgate, "Flee to the mountain like a sparrow." The Arabic also has مثل العصفور [mithl al-ʿuṣfūr], like a sparrow. And Apollinaris in [col. 153] his Metaphrase:
Στρουθὸν ὀρεσσιβότοισιν ὅπως θρώσκοντα νομῆσι, [Strouthon oressibotoisin hopōs thrōskonta nomēsi]

"Like a sparrow leaping in mountain pastures." And Theodoret in his Commentary: Τί δή ποτέ φησι παραινεῖτέ μοι φυγεῖν, καὶ τὰ ὄρη περινοστεῖν στρουθίου δίκην ἐπτοημένου; [Ti dē pote phēsi paraineite moi phygein, kai ta orē perinostein strouthiou dikēn eptoēmenou?] "Why," he says, "do you urge me to flee and wander over the mountains like a frightened sparrow?" But Jerome does better, as I at least think, with "Fly over to the mountain like a bird", as do most of the more recent interpreters. For the sparrow is not a mountain bird. And David, who is the subject here, says that Saul is pursuing him as one would hunt, not a sparrow, but the bird Kore in the mountains, 1 Sam. XXVI, 20, that is, the woodcock, as we have shown. It would be vain to object that near Lake Larius in Italy there is a bird which they call the mountain sparrow. For that bird is not truly a sparrow, but of the blackbird kind, as Gesner proves at length, p. 608. Nor is this passage of Galen, De ingenio sanitatis ch. 2, more to the point: "Among birds, partridges are praised, together with all mountain sparrows." For there not sparrows properly so called are meant, which are very hot and incite lust, but those small birds in general that live in the mountains. For it is agreed that small birds are sometimes called στρουθία [strouthia]. Moschopulus, Περὶ σχεδῶν [Peri schedōn] p. 178: Τρώγλη· ἡ τρύπα, ἀφ᾽ οὗ τρωγλίτης, ὃς καὶ στρουθὸς λέγεται· στρουθία δὲ οὐδετέρως πάντα τὰ μικρὰ τῶν ὀρνίθων. [Trōglē; hē trypa, aph᾽ hou trōglitēs, hos kai strouthos legetai; strouthia de oudeterōs panta ta mikra tōn ornithōn.] So also Phavorinus under Στρουθία [Strouthia].

IV. The fourth passage is Ps. LXXXIV, 4. גם צפור מצאה בית, for which the Greeks have Καὶ γὰρ στρουθίον εὗρεν ἑαυτῷ οἰκίαν [Kai gar strouthion heuren heautō oikian]. And the Arabic in the same sense: لان العصفور وجد له مسكنا [li-anna al-ʿuṣfūr wajada lahu maskanan]. And the Vulgate translator: "For the sparrow has found itself a home." And Jerome: "Since the sparrow has found a home." And Kimchi in his Lexicon proves from this passage that צפור tsippor is not a general name for all birds but proper to a certain species, because in the following hemistich דרור deror is the swallow, as he at least asserts. "Therefore," he says, אחר שאחרון פרט הראשון גם כן פרט, [II, 730] "since the latter (that is, דרור deror) is the name of a particular bird, so also is the former (namely צפור tsippor)." Accordingly in his Commentaries he likewise holds that צפור there is the little bird which the Spaniards call פשׂרא paxaro, that is, the sparrow. So this verse is to be rendered according to Kimchi's mind: "Even the sparrow has found a home, and the swallow a nest for herself, where she may lay her young, namely your altars, O God of hosts." We agree with this view, except that we have interpreted דרור deror as the wood pigeon instead of the swallow. And by the name altars, by synecdoche of part for whole, we have understood the tabernacle, on whose beams both sparrows and wood pigeons nested, as has already been said elsewhere.

V. The fifth passage is Psal. CII, 8. "I have kept watch, and I have become כצפור בודד על גג", where the Greeks have ὡσεὶ στρουθίον μονάζων ἐπὶ δώματι· [hōsei strouthion monazōn epi dōmati], and the Vulgate translator, "like a solitary sparrow on the roof"; and one of the Arabic versions, "I was in my solitude كالعصفور [ka-l-ʿuṣfūr] like a sparrow upon the roof"; and the other, "I have become like a sparrow that stays alone upon the roof." And Apollinaris:
Ἢ στρουθόν τιν᾽ ἄϋπνον ἐόντ᾽ ἐν δώματι μοῦνον, [Ē strouthon tin᾽ aypnon eont᾽ en dōmati mounon]
